prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us ranked B012 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The case rests on a complete chain from physiology to patient benefit: GLP-1 as a gut-derived incretin (Holst), the biology of the proglucagon-derived peptides and their actions (Drucker), and identification of the bioactive 7-36 peptide (Mojsov). That chain produced a drug class with large randomized outcome trials in type 2 diabetes and obesity and documented cardiovascular and renal benefit. The mechanism is stable, independently confirmed over many years, and the recognition is timely. The three-person configuration separates basic physiological discovery from industrial optimisation, which keeps the citation defensible.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is entangled with the work of Habener and others who are not on the shortlisted credit, and the three-person limit excludes Knudsen, whose liraglutide and semaglutide work is what made the biology a durable medicine. A prize that honours the discovery but not the drug-making risks looking incomplete, and a prize that includes the drug-makers cannot stay within three people. There is also a risk that the committee treats this as a foregone conclusion and does not test the attribution as carefully as it would for a contested candidate.

responses.point: Per ranks BCR-ABL inhibition (B016) second, as an exceptional and well-documented path from target to patient that established the paradigm of molecularly targeted cancer therapy.
responses.response: I agree that the clinical consequence is unambiguous and the maturity is beyond doubt. My reservation is about what the prize would reward. Per notes that credit for the underlying BCR-ABL oncogene biology sits outside the credited trio, so a Druker, Lydon and Sawyers prize honours drug development and clinical proof of concept while the discovery of the target stays with others who are not named. I rank it seventh for that reason. I do not think it is a weak candidate. I think its attribution is harder to defend than the GLP-1 trio, where the physiology and the peptide identification are themselves credited.

responses.point: Thomas proposes the three basic-science names for GLP-1, and notes that Mojsov's priority is contested and that drug development (Knudsen) cannot be accommodated within three people.
responses.response: I share this configuration, and his candour about the Mojsov question is the right starting point. Where I would press further is on whether excluding Knudsen is defensible or merely convenient. My view is that it is defensible. The Nobel criterion is a discovery, and the discoveries about incretin physiology and the active peptide precede and enable the pharmaceutical engineering. I would not extend the prize to the drug-makers by loosening the three-person limit. I would, however, want the citation worded so that it does not imply that the basic scientists made the drugs.

responses.point: Rickard places the unfolded protein response (B024) second and optogenetics (B022) third, arguing that a basic-discovery prize does not need clinical translation, and that Walter and Mori are the clean pair.
responses.response: I agree that Walter and Mori are a clean and well-confirmed pair, and I ranked B024 fourth, so I take it seriously. I do not accept that the absence of translation is neutral. The pathway is conceptually deep, but the disease-relevant payoff remains largely prospective, and I weigh that against a candidate whose mechanism has already changed treatment. On optogenetics I am more sceptical than Rickard. Attribution there is the main problem: the split between channelrhodopsin identification (Nagel, Hegemann, Bamberg) and neuronal deployment (Deisseroth, Boyden, Miesenboeck) cannot be cut into three names without a visible injustice, and I ranked it eighth.

responses.point: Abdel ranks CAR-T (B009) second with June and Sadelain only, treating Rosenberg's adoptive cell therapy as influential but a different strand, and flags that Eshhar's concept is missing from the credited set.
responses.response: I think the two-name version is the more defensible one and I would move toward it. In my opening I included Rosenberg, but Abdel's point that adoptive cell transfer is a separate lineage from receptor design is persuasive, and it avoids implying that Rosenberg's TIL work is the same achievement as costimulated CARs. The Eshhar problem remains and I do not think a two-name credit resolves it. For that reason I keep B009 as an alternative rather than my preferred choice, even though it is the strongest second candidate.

responses.point: Sten places CAR-T second and describes the incretin story as a rare combination of basic physiology, peptide chemistry and very large clinical impact.
responses.response: I agree with the description of B012. I differ on ordering at the second position because I place TNF blockade (B046) ahead of CAR-T. Anti-TNF therapy established that blocking one cytokine can control a chronic autoimmune disease, and it has more than twenty years of independent confirmation across several diseases and drug classes. CAR-T has newer evidence and unresolved questions on durability, toxicity and solid tumours. This is a difference in weighting maturity, not in the importance of either.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to identifying the active GLP-1 peptide is credited as an independent discovery, given the contested priority with Habener and others who are not on the credited list.
Whether the committee is comfortable excluding Knudsen and other industrial developers, and how the citation should be worded to avoid overstating what the three basic scientists achieved.
Whether the TNF pair would be seen as basic enough, since Feldmann and Maini's work is mechanistic and clinical but followed earlier TNF biology by others.
Whether a two-part prize pairing GLP-1 with a second, distinct achievement is better than a single-achievement prize, given the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the preferred configuration (B012). My field is autoimmunity and rheumatology, which is close to B046 (TNF blockade), but I have no documented personal or institutional connection to Feldmann or Maini. I will note that proximity for the committee and recuse if a connection is identified.
